rv.q: This entire revitalized gothic romance with its 1980s guitar riffs has that invigorating effect.
The main attraction of Masquerade is not its stars, its story or its music of the night; it's the pleasure of re-exploring a property you already know and seeing it from new angles.
This “Masquerade” is silly, frustrating, ethically dubious and frankly thrilling.
There’s only so much you can “elevate” about a work that fundamentally wants to revel in some schlocky mud.

That’s something new, although the show, which I thought a tad too long, also wants to deliver at those signature Lloyd Webber ditties and thus the result falls uneasily between a new narrative and a new way of telling an old story for the faithful.
This reconfigured Phantom may be closer to a ride than high art, but it sure gives you a closeup look at a lot of terrific craft.

Some sections transcend gimmickry and almost approach poetry: Christine, having fainted, rests on a bed in the Phantom’s Phan Cave, and sinister hands emerge from the mattress and pillow, longing to caress her.
Directed by Diane Paulus, Masquerade is a striking show, in which more things are impressive, rather than—as can be the bane of so much immersive theater—exhausting and tiresome.
Ultimately, it’s the intimacy of the environment that makes Masquerade such a special experience.
Across its reimagining of The Phantom of Opera, Masquerade offers a refreshingly vibrant music of the night.
You can either stage “Phantom” in a theater or create a non-narrative funhouse party experience, but trying to do both at once satisfies neither.

The result of this world creation is a truly moving, unforgettable experience that takes you to the darkest depths of the human mind; yet it still provides hope for a brighter future filled with music and light.
Paulus and team have pulled off something miraculous: an immersive evening that retains the essence and dramatic arc of its source material.

cn.t: Paulus's immersive "Phantom" remix divides critics, who praise its atmospheric spectacle and intimate staging but question whether the gimmicky format justifies shuffling audiences through dimly lit hallways for two hours.
